scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

Carthaginian-empire and carthage are two imported labels for one polity. First label covers an early coarse 500–200 BCE map span, with map_coverage retained so its 200 BCE endpoint does not misleadingly assert conquest. Later alias covers a coarse 200–100 BCE span; historical -146 cutoff prevents the page displaying as a living Punic state at 100 BCE. No borders edited or certified.

UNESCO English brief synthesis has a 146 AD typo; its introductory language versions, British Museum, and standard chronology give 146 BCE. Dido is named only as legend. The mixed-period UNESCO property includes Roman monuments, which are explicitly excluded from Punic attribution.

Kerkuane is a separate Punic town and illustrative comparison, not a claimed Carthage house excavation. Its visible houses are late fourth/early third century BCE and local bath features cannot be generalized to all Punic homes. Bir Massouda latrines are structures interpreted in a published excavation abstract; no flush mechanism or prevalence invented.

Louvre AO5175 inscription is attested in Latin-letter epigraphic transliteration. The Phoenician Unicode letter sequence in the card is a letter-for-letter modern rendering of the first two words, with vowels omitted, not a facsimile of stone letter shapes. The final inscription words remain undeciphered. Reading a formal stela does not imply mass literacy.

Cambridge book frontmatter figure catalogue identifies a feeding bottle but gives no residue analysis, user identity, or typical childcare practice. Mago’s 28-book original is lost and authorship uncertain; the card does not claim the original manuscript survives. KAI074 is a fragmentary tariff translated by DEAPS, not a comprehensive account of Punic worship.

No exact Roman Republic successor link was added because imported event-year geometry and annexation associations require separate verification. Conquest and subsequent Roman city are narrated with sources. Source-checked author draft remains pending independent review.

proposedOverrides.summary: Punic Carthage grew into a major western Mediterranean trading and naval power. Its houses, writing, coins and sanitation reveal more than Hannibal’s wars. Rome destroyed the city in 146 BCE; a Roman city later rose on the site, while Punic traditions did not disappear with one capital.

sharedAssociations.basis: The two imported labels represent consecutive map slices of the same Punic Carthage, with a historically attested political ending in 146 BCE. Shared narrative is not a claim that the imported polygons are exact borders.
